findings.where: The full-width blue 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band with its white 'Subscribe' button, directly under the hero (desktop-02 top, phone-01)
findings.fault: The page shows a second main action straight after the hero. It is set in the strongest colour field on the page, with a heading almost as large as Mark's line, so it outweighs the 'Write to me directly' box. The heading also speaks of Mark in the third person ('Mark's briefings') after a first-person hero, and it promises a briefing service that the brief nowhere says exists.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief asks for one direct, personal way to reach Mark, in his voice, with no invented claims. A visitor from a development bank would also object: they are pulled toward a newsletter sign-up, a sales move, instead of writing to the advisor.

findings.fault: It looks like a button that signs you up, but the parts map shows it is only a link to #subscribe. No subscribe form or section appears anywhere on the page at either width, so pressing it does nothing a visitor can see.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who presses it expecting to sign up gets no form and no confirmation, and is left unsure whether anything happened.

findings.fault: There is no navigation at all, just the name and the logo as a home link. No Articles, About or Contact links exist, though the palette table lists 'nav links' as a use of mist.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief lists nav as part of the first screen. A procurement reader who wants Mark's articles, talks or background also has nowhere to go but scrolling.

findings.where: Article specimen: the two body paragraphs, the subhead 'So, what are the key 'chapter topics'?', the numbered list and the closing paragraph (desktop-04, desktop-05, desktop-06; phone-03, phone-04)
findings.fault: Long reading text is centred. Every line starts at a different point, the list items centre under left-hanging numbers so the numbers float apart from their text, and the left-aligned title and byline sit above centred prose.
findings.who_objects: Anyone reading one of Mark's articles, the page the research calls 'the product', would object, because centred paragraphs are slow and tiring to read. Angélique would object too, since every list she adds will break apart the same way.

findings.where: Hero photograph (desktop-01, phone-01) and the same cut-out in Texture and the Motion sketch
findings.fault: The 'Mark at work' direction depends on him being seen speaking. Here he is keyed out of his backdrop and blown up to a huge floating head, with the lectern, microphone and room scaled or cut away. It reads more like a campaign poster than an advisor at a podium, and the keyed hair edge shows against the slate.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who chose v7 for 'a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking'. A cautious reader at a development bank would also object, because a looming portrait under 'we are at a turning point' reads as salesy or political rather than measured counsel.

findings.where: PDF card at the end of the article specimen ('Streamlining the PPP Process… · PDF', desktop-06, phone-04)
findings.fault: The card shows a download arrow and 'PDF', so it promises a file, but the parts map shows it links to #article. Its look is also unlike anything else on the page: rounded corners, a pale blue fill, a blue hairline border and a wide soft drop shadow, on an otherwise flat, square-cornered page.
findings.who_objects: A reader who clicks to download the lecture gets no file. A designer would also object that the one shadowed, rounded, tinted box looks dropped in from another site, and pairs a hairline border with a wide soft shadow on a resting element.

findings.where: Blue on text that cannot be clicked: the 'PALETTE' label, the article list numbers (desktop-02, desktop-05, phone-01, phone-04)
findings.fault: The house blue marks links and the action, and the article's own note says 'blue only where something can be clicked'. Yet the PALETTE label and the list numbers, neither of them clickable, are set in it.
findings.who_objects: A visitor would object, because blue text that does nothing teaches them that blue is unreliable as a link cue. The founder would object because the tile breaks the rule it states.

findings.where: Section labels below the fold: 'PALETTE' (desktop-02) against 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' (desktop-03 to desktop-06), and 'Texture' (desktop-03)
findings.fault: Parts of the same kind look different. PALETTE is blue, tracked capitals, against the type note's own 'sentence case, never tracked capitals'. Three sections take a small grey sans label. Texture has no label at all, only a large italic serif heading.
findings.who_objects: The founder, reading the specimen as a system, sees a set of styles that do not agree. They would doubt that the type rules shown will hold on the real site.

findings.fault: The caption naming the photograph sits at the far left under the action, the whole width of the line away from the photograph on the right. At a glance it belongs to the text block, not the photo.
findings.who_objects: The founder, reading the first screen, does not connect the stand-in note with the photograph it explains.

findings.where: Display headings 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' and 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform'
findings.fault: The apostrophes look straight, while the article body uses typographer's curly quotes. Up close, the two largest serif lines look set by machine.
findings.who_objects: A reader with an eye for type would see it at display size, on a site whose whole look rests on refined serif setting.

findings.fault: It is a button (it replays the motion here), but it is styled as an underlined text link, the treatment the page uses for navigation.
findings.who_objects: Few would notice. A keyboard or screen-reader user expecting a link to go somewhere would find it acts in place instead.
